answer: Proof-of-personhood mining resists Sybil attacks by requiring each identity to lock a durable bond that is slashed on misbehavior. Copying identities is cheap, but each needs its own stake, so an attacker's cost scales linearly with account count. The economics turn a mirror onto the attacker: splitting gains are outweighed by capital frozen and forfeited. A reef of colluding accounts becomes an expense, since shared funding lets the protocol burn the bonded set. Honest holders pay once; a spiral of fakes just sinks obligations. Influence itself is priced, not registry trust.
